_comment: Polynesian expansion batch 168 - Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, Gutenberg #66357 (1917): ch. 3 (The Water of Life / Aukele cycle), ch. 4 (A Viking of the Pacific / Hawaii-loa), ch. 7 (Paao from Samoa). Topics 3 heroic, 4 founding. All passages are labeled paraphrase.

title.en: Aukele Wins the Water of Life in the Far-off Helani
title.zh: 奧克勒遠國取生命之水

region.zh: 遙遠的海拉尼（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (New York 1917)

summary.en: The Self-reliant Dragon arms the youngest son Aukele with a bamboo stick holding Lono's image, a food-leaf, and her own skin - a cloak that shatters enemies into ashes. His warrior brothers wreck the mission by calling their boat a war canoe and are destroyed; Aukele alone survives to marry the chiefess, defeat the cannibal god Ku-waha-ilo - father of Pele - and, grieving for his drowned brothers, fly toward the sunrise for Kane's living water: past the moon ancestress whose food thins her to a new moon, into the pit of watchmen, past the dirty calabash, to the pure water of life which sprinkles his brothers back to standing.
summary.zh: 自信龍神以竹杖賜予幼子奧克勒：內藏龍諾神像、取之不竭的食葉與她自剝的神皮——披之則敵化飛灰。好戰的兄長們自毀使命、命喪海底；唯奧克勒倖存，娶得女酋，擊敗佩蕾之父——食人神庫瓦希伊洛。為救溺亡的兄長，他朝日出行空遠征：途經啃薄自己化為新月的月亮祖母，躍過守水者的深坑，辨別濁水與真水，終以生命之水灑海，喚起沉船中的兄弟。

passages.text: The Self-reliant Dragon is frequently mentioned in the oldest Hawaiian legends; she dwelt in one of the mysterious islands mentioned in the Hawaiian chants as Kua-i-Helani, the Far-away Helani, lying in the ancient far western home of the Polynesians. Iku was the chief, and the youngest of his sons was Aukele-nui-a-Iku, Aukele the Great Son of Iku. Aukele was a favorite of the Self-reliant Dragon; she gave him a large bamboo stick, inside which she placed an image of the god Lono, and also a magic leaf which could provide plenty of food for any one who touched the leaf to his lips, and put in a part of her own skin. She said, 'This skin is a cloak for you. If you lift it up against any enemies, they will fall to pieces as dust and ashes.' The brothers, who were great warriors, determined to sail away, find a new land and conquer it by fighting; Aukele persuaded them to take him.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: After a long time on the sea all their food was gone and they were starving and lying in the bottom of the boat; Aukele fed them from the leaf which he touched to their lips. Some days passed and Aukele said, 'To-morrow we will come to a land where a woman is the ruler; let me tell why we journey.' The chiefess of that land looked out and saw a boat in the ocean, and sent some birds to see what the boat was doing and learn whether it was a war canoe or a travelling boat; Aukele wanted his brothers to say it was a travelling boat, but the birds asked and the brothers said, 'This is a war canoe.' The birds went away. Aukele took up the bamboo stick and threw it in the sea, and leaped in after it. The brothers threw the cloak of Aukele on the beach; the chiefess found the cloak and shook it toward the boat, then threw it away - the brothers broke into small dust and were destroyed, the boat and the brothers sinking to the bottom of the sea. Aukele swam to the beach, pulled up his stick, found his cloak, lay down under a tree and slept.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: A watchdog came out and smelled the man and barked; the chiefess called two women and told them to see who it was and, if they found any one, kill him. The women came and he greeted them, knowing their names; they were ashamed because he had found their names, and one said, 'What can we give him for naming us?' - 'We will let him be the husband of our ruler.' The chiefess turned the dog out again; at once there was more barking, and she told her bird brothers to go and look over the land. Lono told Aukele: 'When they come you say their names quickly and welcome them.' This knowledge gave him power over them, and they could not harm him. When he went up to the house he stood at the door; the dog ran out and tried to bite Aukele through the magic cloak, and the dog became ashes. The brothers came with food put in moss-covered calabashes; he never touched it - it was the death food; he went to where green calabash vines were growing, took a calabash, broke it and found good food inside. Then they lived as man and wife; the chiefess had been a cannibal but at this time stopped eating men. Soon a son was born.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The chiefess told her brothers to go away into the heavens and find her father, Ku-waha-ilo, a cannibal god, also the father of Pele, the goddess of volcanic fire. The father saw Aukele flying and was angry. Lono told Aukele to put on his magic cloak; the cannibal father made fire, called Kuku-ena, the lightning, and Ikuwa, a stone crashing like thunder; the lightning and the crashing stone were struck by the cloak and rattled into ashes. After the battle the bird brothers told their father that the daughter was well and this was her husband. After this flight and this victory over the cannibal god, Aukele returned to his wife. After a time the ghosts of his brothers appeared to him and reminded him of their grave in the sea; Aukele ate nothing for days, and his wife told him if he had strength enough to find the living water of Kane he could still restore his brothers. She made a straight line toward the East, the sunrise, and told him to fly straight, not swerving to either side.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: He thought he was flying in a straight line, but one arm became tired because the stick was under it; he changed the stick, and this moved his direction. His god saw this and told him he was leaving the straight line and flying to some other place. There was fire far below; all the people had fled except one. 'Let us go straight till we come to that one; then you catch him and hold him fast; we shall have life.' This was the moon, who was an ancestress of his wife; the moon had been cooking food, and she arose to take up her food and get ready to go; but Aukele caught her, held her and ate her food - she thus became thin, a new moon, and the traveller gained strength to return to his home. Aukele tried again according to his wife's line: he flew straight a long time until he found a strange land with a deep pit lined with trees and wonderful plants, at the bottom the spring of the water of life. He leaped down upon the back of a watchman on the edge of the pit, who had been put there to kill any one coming after the water; 'Who are you? My grandchild, the brother of Pele, never got on my back. Who are you?' Aukele gave his name and ancestors, and told the watchman he had come for the water of life for his brothers.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The watchman told him to fly to another watchman, who told him to go straight to the bottom of the pit: 'There a blind woman will be sitting. Look at the place where she is cooking bananas. She will take them one by one; you eat all her bananas. Then she will become angry and throw ashes; if she throws on the right side you must fly to the left; watch if she strikes with a stick, then run quickly, sit in her lap, and tell her who you are.' When he had done all these things and all attempts to kill him had failed, Aukele made the old blind woman lie down under a cocoanut tree, got two young cocoanuts and told her to turn her eyes toward the sky; he dropped the cocoanuts in her eyes; she wept sorely because of the pain, rubbed the water out of her eyes and said, 'I can see you.' She told him what he must do to get the water of life: bring the stem of a water plant and a bush with white flowers; she squeezed the water from the plants into a cup, took charcoal and mixed them until black, then painted Aukele's hands very black, like the hands of the brother of Pele - those watching the water of life would look at the hands reaching for water and make no mistake; they would tightly cover up the water if a white hand came down. 'Wait until the guardian god is asleep; then go to the door and one will give you some water. The first will be dirty water; throw it away. Put your hand down again; they will give you another calabash of water. This will be the living water of Kane; take it.' He went down and put his hand in for the water; the watchman handed out a calabash of dirty water, he threw it away and again thrust his black hand down the pit, and the watchman gave him a calabash of the pure water of life. He flew rapidly along the path to the outside world; in his haste he struck the leaves of the groves of trees, and the sound swept through the land of the water of life like rolling thunder. The brother of Pele and his servants awoke and followed, but Aukele fled through the heavens to the place where the ghosts of his brothers lay in the sunken ship. The chiefess told her husband to pour the water of life in his hand; she put her fingers in the water and sprinkled drops over the sea. Out in the ocean under the moving surface was a boat, its mast coming up through the waves; in a little while they saw men standing in the boat - these were the brothers of Aukele. After the welcome, he gave them lands and homes. In that strange far-off land of the ancestors - the mysterious Floating Island, the Hidden Island of Kane - it is said they still live under the rule of their younger brother.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 3 (1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Hawaii-loa, the First Viking of the Pacific
title.zh: 夏威夷洛亞：太平洋首位航海王

region.en: Land of Kane to Hawaiian islands (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 卡內之土至夏威夷群島（象徵性定位）

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (New York 1917)

summary.en: The Polynesian meles rival the Viking sagas: bold expeditions, stirring adventures, voyages to far-off lands, naming each new country. In the long chant of Kumu Honua, the first created, Hawaii-loa is the first sea-king of the Polynesians, reported as making long journeys and discovering the Hawaiian Islands - an ancestor of islands rather than of families, who lived in the land of the handsome golden god Kane, near the green precipiced paradise where the water of life gave forth healing even for the dead.
summary.zh: 波利尼西亞之歌可與北歐維京薩迦媲美：壯舉與遠航層見疊出，所到之地皆以己意命名。在『初造者』庫穆霍努阿的長篇頌歌中，夏威夷洛亞是波利尼西亞首位海上王者——遠航發現夏威夷群島，成為島嶼而非宗族之祖。他居於金神卡內的土地，鄰近生命之水湧流、連死者亦可癒合的翠崖樂園。

sensitivity.note: Ethnogenetic tradition; Westervelt's Viking comparison retained as framing.

passages.text: History is frequently legendary. Legends are the indistinct memories of nations, and are of real value when there is any opportunity for comparison. Early Norse history was told in song legends; the sagas of the Vikings are rivalled in some measure by the meles of the Hawaiians. The Hawaiians have both the chant - the mele, and the tradition - the olelo; from these come Hawaiian ancient history. The Vikings, sea kings, the men who sailed out from the vicks, the fjords of the Scandinavian coast, were brave mariners; they swept the European coast, infested Mediterranean waters, found the North Atlantic islands, and named the countries newly discovered after their own fancies. The Polynesian folklore abounds in stories of remarkable men, bold expeditions, stirring adventures and voyages to far-off lands; the Vikings of the Pacific gave to their foreign lands the names by which these lands were then known and by which they are known to-day.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the long Hawaiian chant of Kumu Honua, the first created, there is a part devoted to Hawaii-loa, the first sea-king of the Polynesians. He is reported as making long journeys and discovering the Hawaiian Islands; besides this chant there are many legends and references which make him an important ancestor among Hawaiians, an ancestor of islands rather than of families. He lived in the land of the handsome or golden god Kane; to the north lay the land Ulu-nui, the Great Ulu; his home was near the green precipiced paradise of Hawaiian legend, the place where the water of life gave forth healing even for the dead.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 4 (1917); not verbatim.

title.en: Paao Sails from Samoa to the Voice of Hawaii
title.zh: 帕阿奧自薩摩亞循聲赴夏威夷

region.en: Upolu, Samoa, to Puna, Hawaii (symbolic pin)
region.zh: 自薩摩亞烏波盧至夏威夷普納（象徵性定位）

texts.period: Hawaiian tradition dated c. 1100 CE; retold 1917 (Westervelt)

source.work: W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (New York 1917)

summary.en: On Upolu the priest Paao, accused by his elder brother Lonopele of fruit-theft, slays his own son and opens his stomach to prove innocence - then, in anger, kills Lonopele's son and flees north. Storms, a magic bird pouring waves, fish pushing the boats, and at last a wind with no salt in it: 'I hear no voice - Hawaii! Hawaii!! and the strong voice of the Maile blossoms... The fingers of the morning touch the mountains of Hawaii.' He lands in state, builds Wahaula temple, and his priestly line runs to Hewahewa, who burned the same temples seven hundred years later.
summary.zh: 烏波盧島祭司帕阿奧遭兄長誣子竊果，竟剖愛子之腹以自證清白——繼而憤殺兄子，舉族北逃。途中風暴驟起、魔鳥傾浪、群魚推舟，直至聞得那無鹹味的風：『夏威夷！夏威夷！邁蕾花香嘹亮，甘蔗低吟，麵包果呼喚——晨曦的手指已觸到夏威夷的群山。』他盛裝登陸，建瓦豪拉神廟；其祭司世系綿延至赫瓦赫瓦——七百年後親手焚毀同廟之人。

sensitivity.note: Child-sacrifice episode recorded as in the tradition; Paao is the traditional founder of the Hawaiian high-priest line.

passages.text: Hawaiians never reckoned history by dates, but by genealogies, as did the Hebrews; they measured time not by the years but by the lives of men, not by the days passed but by the deeds done. When Ka-meha-meha became king of the Rainbow Islands his royal chant took the supreme place: he traced his royal blood to Pili, from a foreign land, and through Pili back to Wa-kea, a Polynesian chief of perhaps the second century, and thence back through a series of hero-gods to Kumu-Honua, the first created. Not far from the year 1100 A.D., two priest brothers were living on Upolu, one of the Samoan Islands: Lonopele, the elder, lived in one of the luxurious valleys opening upon the seacoast; Paao, the younger, was a seaman as well as a priest, and lived near the beach, where he kept a small fleet of canoes.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In some way bitter feeling arose between the two households. One day Lonopele came to the temple where his brother was making ready to sacrifice a sacred black hog, and cried, 'Where are you, O Paao, that you prepare a sacrifice for the favour of the gods, when you do not watch your oldest boy? Some of my choice fruits, brought from Tahiti, are beginning to ripen; and each night Kaino, your son, creeps under the low branches and gathers whatever is good.' 'It is false!' angrily replied the father. Theft was considered the greatest of crimes among the Polynesians. 'No! It is true. He is coming even now from his feast. If he touches my fruit again he shall die. It is tabu.' The boy came near, evidently having just been eating. 'Have you taken fruit from Lonopele in the night?' 'No. I have fruit at home, but better are the baked dog and fish; I would not eat his fruit.' Lonopele became angry and cried out: 'May the god, Kanaloa, curse you and break your body into fragments, for your falsehood.' 'Cut open my stomach, O my uncle, and I shall be proved innocent.' Paao determined to substitute his son for the sacrifice he was preparing, and thus prove his guilt or innocence; no trace of fruit was found in the body. Lonopele bowed his head in shame and hastened away. The Hawaiian traditions say that after this act he determined to leave Upolu, and agreed with a few trusted friends to prepare their large canoes and go with him, seeking the Burning-Java, or Hawaii, somewhere toward the north.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The sides of the boats were to be built two or three feet higher, hewing boards with stone axes and sewing them to each other through holes drilled by bones, using cords of cocoanut fibre for thread - thus canoes were prepared capable of carrying thirty to sixty persons; dried bananas, pigs, fish and pounded taro were made ready. One day Paao saw his brother's son coming near the boats, and in a fit of anger rushed upon the boy and slew him. Lonopele soon discovered the murder and made war upon Paao. Paao and his friends launched their canoes as fast as possible, placing in them their families and such provisions as were at hand; his warriors, defeated by Lonopele, hastened to the canoes and shoved out into the deep waters. The battle was evidently fierce, for the legends say that some of the prophet friends who could not escape to their canoes leaped from the precipitous cliffs to fly to the boats, and were dashed to pieces on the rocks below. One of the priest-friends leaped into the water, calling for Paao to return and rescue him. 'Not so', answered Paao, 'we have left the shore; it would be an evil omen to turn back. We will wait for you where we are.' The legends say the priest flew like a bird to the canoes and was warmly received. Lonopele sent a storm to destroy the canoes; two great fish aided the fugitives - the Aku pushed the boats, and the Opelea hindered the storm waves by opposing his great body and breaking their force. Lonopele ordered his magic bird to take up great waves of water and pour them from the sky, overwhelming the fugitives; the canoe-men hurriedly arranged mats covering the boats, and the water was turned into the sea. Thus they escaped.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: The days passed; sometimes showers fell upon the mats arranged like funnels, filling the water calabashes afresh; sometimes they passed through a school of fish and caught all they could, drying them for future use; some died and descended to the bountiful islands in the world under the waters; some of the canoes were abandoned. One day Paao said: 'I was watching the stars last night and my thought is that some water-god has put his hands under our boats and moved us away from Hawaii.' That night Paao could not sleep; he studied the stars; he felt a breeze that seemed to him in some way different from the ordinary sea-breezes. 'Do you feel the new wind from the eastern star?' he said softly to his steersmen. 'Aye! we have to hold the steering paddles more firmly.' Paao awakened his prophet and whispered: 'Does the new wind have a voice for you?' The prophet sniffed the air, then stepped upon the high prow and breathed again. 'Aye, the wind has the voice of smoke, perhaps the smoke of the burning-mountain. Say nothing about the voice; we will change our course and sail toward the bright star.'
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.

passages.text: In the very early morning of the third day, as Paao was restlessly looking eastward, his wife crept to his side: 'O my Paao, I am about to die. I have just dreamed of the green-walled paradise; I smelled the sweet Maile blossoms and the leaves of our marriage wreath; I saw the spirits of my sons stand by the cocoanut tree. The vision is from the gods; I must surely die.' 'Hush', said Paao quickly, 'I too have heard the voice of the Maile born on the winds but I was awake. You shall not die. Call the astrologer, and then listen to his words.' The astrologer came quickly; Paao handed his friend a calabash with a little precious water, bidding him bathe his parched mouth and nostrils. 'Now what do the winds say?' 'Hawaii! Hawaii!! and the strong voice of the Maile blossoms, and the gentle voice of the sugar-cane. I can hear the bread-fruit call Come and eat. The Lau-hala's voice comes over the sea. Awake, awake, oh canoe-men! The fingers of the morning touch the mountains of Hawaii; the morning is raising its hand to beckon us on. O friends of the canoes, awake! Hear the land voices. Hear the wind that has no salt in it. Awake and hear Hawaii.' In a moment shouts and songs of gladness were heard from all the canoes; new life, new strength pervaded the weakened wanderers, and the steersmen unconsciously changed the course of the boats toward the blue haze of land outlined by the dawn. Bundles of feather robes were unrolled; native cloth, brilliantly coloured, was taken from its wrappings; Paao robed himself in a high-priest's tabu mantle of black feathers, wearing a white helmet ornamented with black plumes. Thus, as the new morning dawned, they came to Hawaii; thus they landed as if their journey had known nothing of starvation and death. The language of the newcomers was almost identical in meaning and pronunciation with the native tongue; the priests with new gods were received with offerings, food and clothing in abundance were given, and land in Puna, near Hilo, was set apart for their dwelling-place. Paao, aided by the Hawaiians, at once built a temple at Wahaula, which after being twice restored was destroyed in 1820. From Paao the high priest's family, highest in priestly rank of all dwelling in the islands, was perpetuated until Ka-meha-meha's high priest, Hewa-hewa, a lineal descendant of Paao, in 1819 aided in destroying the temples of the gods - with his own hands Hewa-hewa set fire to shrines and idols, overthrowing the system of worship and sacred tabu which Paao had established nearly 700 years before.
passages.note: Paraphrase of W. D. Westervelt, Hawaiian Historical Legends, ch. 7 (1917); not verbatim.
